lessons.title: Homeostasis and temperature control
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Homeostasis; nervous and hormonal coordination; excretion (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the control of body temperature in a mammal.
reviewNotes: Fever example is a simplified description; clinical details are not covered.
Brown fat and hormonal effects are outlined only.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Homeostasis
blocks.md: **Homeostasis** is the maintenance of a stable internal environment (temperature, blood glucose, water potential, pH) within narrow limits, despite changes outside. A control loop has a **set point**, **receptors** that detect deviation, a **control centre** (coordinator) and **effectors** that bring about a correction. **Negative feedback** reverses a change; **positive feedback** amplifies it (e.g. contractions in childbirth).

blocks.title: Both directions of correction
blocks.md: Control needs effectors for **both** directions of change (e.g. warming and cooling). Do not describe only the response to heat. Also remember that the **hypothalamus** detects temperature of the blood and receives input from skin thermoreceptors; it does not itself sweat. Vasodilation does not 'move arterioles closer to the skin': the vessels widen so more blood flows through the skin capillaries.

blocks.caption: Negative feedback control of body temperature when too hot.
blocks.alt: Four boxes around a ring: temperature rises, receptors detect it, effectors act, and the temperature falls back.

blocks.title: Response to heat and cold
blocks.md: **Too hot**: vasodilation, sweating, hairs lie flat, lower metabolic rate, behaviour (shade). **Too cold**: vasoconstriction, no sweat, hair erector muscles raise hairs (traps air), shivering, adrenaline/thyroxine raise metabolic rate, behaviour (curl up, huddle). Brown fat in some young mammals releases heat directly.

blocks.title: Endotherms and ectotherms
blocks.md: **Endotherms** (birds, mammals) make heat internally and keep a nearly constant core temperature; they need more food. **Ectotherms** (reptiles, amphibians, fish, insects) depend on environmental heat and behaviour; they need less food and can survive on less. Both have enzymes with an optimum temperature, which is why temperature control matters.

blocks.title: Worked example — rate of rise
blocks.statement: During exercise a runner's core temperature rises from 37.0 °C to 38.6 °C in 20 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of rise.

blocks.title: Worked example — feedback loop
blocks.statement: A person at Mount Cameroon at night begins to shiver and the skin looks pale. Explain with negative feedback.
steps: Falling blood temperature is detected by the hypothalamus.
Effectors: skeletal muscles shiver (heat) and skin arterioles constrict (pallor, less heat loss).
Blood temperature rises back to the set point and the effectors switch off.

objectives: Explain the resting potential and the action potential.
Describe the transmission of impulses along axons and across synapses.
reviewNotes: Threshold −55 mV, peak +40 mV and the 3:2 pump ratio are standard textbook values.
Chemical synapse described is the cholinergic type; other transmitters not covered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Resting and action potential
blocks.md: At rest the inside of a neurone is about **−70 mV** relative to the outside. The **Na⁺/K⁺ pump** moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in; the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺ (K⁺ leaks out). A stimulus that reaches the **threshold** (about −55 mV) opens **voltage-gated Na⁺ channels**: Na⁺ floods in (**depolarisation**, up to about +40 mV). Na⁺ channels close and **K⁺ channels** open: K⁺ leaves (**repolarisation**), often briefly overshooting (hyperpolarisation).

blocks.title: All-or-nothing
blocks.md: An action potential is **all-or-nothing**: below threshold nothing happens; above threshold the size is always the same. A stronger stimulus gives a **higher frequency** of impulses, not a bigger impulse. The **refractory period** (Na⁺ channels temporarily unable to open) makes impulses discrete and one-way. Do not confuse **resting potential** (maintained by the pump) with the action potential (caused by voltage-gated channels).

blocks.caption: The action potential: resting level, threshold, rapid depolarisation to about +40 mV and repolarisation.
blocks.alt: A line graph of membrane potential against time with a sharp red spike from −70 mV up to +40 mV and back below resting level.

blocks.title: Conduction and synapse
blocks.md: A local circuit of ions depolarises the next section of the axon. In **myelinated** neurones the impulse jumps between **nodes of Ranvier** (saltatory conduction, faster and less energy). At a **cholinergic synapse**: impulse arrives, **Ca²⁺ channels open**, vesicles fuse and release **acetylcholine**, which diffuses across the cleft, binds receptors and opens Na⁺ channels in the postsynaptic membrane. The transmitter is broken down by acetylcholinesterase.

blocks.title: Speed and reflexes
blocks.md: Speed is greater in **wider** axons, **myelinated** axons and at **higher temperature**. A **reflex arc**: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the spinal cord → motor neurone → effector. Reflexes are fast and automatic, protecting the body (e.g. withdrawing a hand from a hot object).

blocks.title: Worked example — speed
blocks.statement: An impulse travels 0.50 m along a myelinated motor neurone in 5.0 ms. Calculate the speed.

blocks.title: Worked example — frequency
blocks.statement: A neurone fires 25 impulses in 0.5 s when lightly stimulated and 75 when strongly stimulated. Compare the frequencies.
steps: The size of each impulse is unchanged; only frequency increases (3 times).

lessons.title: Hormones and the control of blood glucose
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Homeostasis; nervous and hormonal coordination; excretion (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the roles of insulin, glucagon and adrenaline.
Explain negative feedback in the control of blood glucose.
Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes and interpret a glucose tolerance test.
reviewNotes: Normal blood glucose range varies between sources (fasting about 4–6 mmol dm⁻³); health content must be reviewed by a health professional.
Patient data in the problem are illustrative, not real measurements.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Endocrine system
blocks.md: **Hormones** are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands, carried in the blood to **target cells** with specific receptors. Effects are slower and longer-lasting than nervous effects. In the pancreas the **islets of Langerhans** contain **β cells** (make insulin) and **α cells** (make glucagon). Blood glucose is normally kept at roughly 4–6 mmol dm⁻³ (a typical teaching range; check the figure used locally).

blocks.title: Insulin and glucagon
blocks.md: **High glucose**: β cells release **insulin**; target cells (liver, muscle, fat) take up more glucose through more glucose carriers, convert glucose to **glycogen** (glycogenesis) and respire more. **Low glucose**: α cells release **glucagon**: liver converts glycogen to glucose (**glycogenolysis**) and makes glucose from amino acids and glycerol (**gluconeogenesis**). **Adrenaline** also raises glucose.

blocks.caption: Negative feedback control of blood glucose after a meal.
blocks.alt: Four boxes around a ring: glucose rises, beta cells release insulin, liver and muscle take up glucose, glucose falls.

blocks.title: Insulin and glucagon act as a pair
blocks.md: Do not say 'insulin turns glucose into glycogen' without saying that it acts on the **liver and muscle cells**, and do not say glucagon is a form of insulin. Negative feedback in both directions: the same pancreas senses the glucose level directly. Type 1 diabetes is an **autoimmune** loss of β cells (insulin injections); type 2 is reduced sensitivity of target cells to insulin, linked to diet, obesity and inactivity (diet, exercise, medicines).

blocks.title: Glucose tolerance test
blocks.md: After fasting, the person drinks a glucose solution and blood glucose is measured at intervals. In a healthy person it rises and returns to the fasting level within about two hours; in a person with diabetes it rises higher and stays high. Urine tests and blood tests are used in screening; interpretation belongs to clinicians.

blocks.title: Worked example — rate of fall
blocks.statement: After a meal a student's blood glucose falls from 9.0 to 5.0 mmol dm⁻³ in 90 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of fall.

blocks.title: Worked example — percentage change
blocks.statement: A diabetic patient's fasting glucose is 8.0 mmol dm⁻³; after treatment it is 5.6. Calculate the percentage decrease.

lessons.title: The kidney: excretion and osmoregulation
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Homeostasis; nervous and hormonal coordination; excretion (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the structure of the nephron and the processes of ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption.
Explain how the loop of Henlé and ADH control water balance.
reviewNotes: GFR of 125 cm³ min⁻¹ is a standard textbook value; counter-current multiplier detail may exceed the syllabus.
Health-related statements must be reviewed by a health professional.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Nephron and ultrafiltration
blocks.md: Each kidney has about a million **nephrons**. In the **renal capsule** blood in the **glomerulus** (high hydrostatic pressure because the efferent arteriole is narrower than the afferent) forces water, glucose, amino acids, urea and ions through the capillary wall, basement membrane and podocytes into the **Bowman's capsule** (filtrate). **Blood cells and large proteins** stay in the blood. Normal GFR is about 125 cm³ per minute (textbook value).

blocks.title: Reabsorption and loop of Henlé
blocks.md: In the **proximal convoluted tubule** microvilli and many mitochondria allow reabsorption of all glucose and amino acids (active transport), most salts and about 80 % of the water. The **loop of Henlé** (counter-current multiplier) pumps ions into the medulla so that medulla tissue fluid has very low water potential; water leaves the collecting duct by osmosis if the duct is permeable.

blocks.caption: The path of filtrate through the nephron with the main process at each stage.
blocks.alt: Five boxes in a vertical chain from glomerulus to ureter with notes on each stage.

blocks.title: ADH and osmoregulation
blocks.md: If blood water potential falls (dehydration), **osmoreceptors** in the hypothalamus stimulate the posterior pituitary to release **ADH**. ADH makes the distal tubule and collecting duct more permeable to water (more aquaporins), so more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced. If water potential is high, less ADH is released: a large volume of dilute urine.

blocks.title: Filtration is not selective
blocks.md: Ultrafiltration is selective only by **size**; useful substances like glucose enter the filtrate and are reabsorbed later. Urea is a waste made in the liver from excess amino acids (deamination). Do not say the kidney 'filters out blood cells and keeps them in the nephron'; blood cells never leave the capillary. **Dehydration** gives more ADH, not less.

blocks.title: Worked example — filtration per day
blocks.statement: GFR is 125 cm³ per minute. Calculate the volume filtered per day in dm³ (1 dm³ = 1000 cm³).

blocks.title: Worked example — percentage reabsorbed
blocks.statement: In one day 180 dm³ is filtered and 1.5 dm³ of urine is produced. Calculate the percentage of the filtrate reabsorbed.
